links.label: The giver of perfection and divine simplicity
links.rationale: Exercise2 uses the exact maxim that the giver cannot lack what it gives. Nihāya uses it in proving that no existential perfection is absent from the Necessary, while explaining how the possession is compatible with simplicity.

links.label: Complete cause and necessary effect
links.rationale: Muẓaffar’s transition from resemblance to certain demonstration depends on the common feature being a complete cause. Bidāya explains why a complete cause and its effect cannot be separated.

links.label: Complete cause rather than one causal factor
links.rationale: The argument’s certainty requires the full cause. Nihāya distinguishes complete from incomplete causes, including in voluntary action, and argues that the complete cause necessitates its effect.

links.label: Knowing the cause and knowing a caused conclusion
links.rationale: Muẓaffar contrasts bare observation with inquiry that knows a causal explanation. Nihāya develops the dependence of certain knowledge of a caused thing on its cause and distinguishes the case of what has no cause.

It is therefore clear from the foregoing that investigating a conclusion sought yields knowledge of it only by proceeding to it through its cause, if it has a cause, or through general concomitances, if it has no cause. Proceeding to a cause through its effect, however, yields no knowledge at all.
links.qualification: Nihāya separately allows general concomitances for what has no cause and discusses the objection from sensation. This is not an assertion that both authors give an identical modern theory of induction.

links.label: Proof must terminate in self-evident premises
links.rationale: Compound syllogisms are traced back to self-evident premises to avoid an endless regress of acquisition. Bidāya states the same dependence of discursive knowledge on immediate cognition.

links.label: Reductio, contradictories, and the first principle
links.rationale: Muẓaffar’s reductio establishes the target by falsifying its contradictory because contradictories cannot both be false. Nihāya names their joint truth/joint falsity exclusion the first principle and describes the exceptive syllogism completing knowledge.
